mcqs.question: What's the core distinction between Template Method and Strategy?
options: Template Method fixes the algorithm's skeleton and lets a subclass override one step via inheritance; Strategy delegates the entire algorithm to a separately composed, injected object
Template Method and Strategy both require the exact same amount of inheritance
Strategy can only be used with algorithms that have no steps at all
Template Method is only usable in languages without interfaces
mcqs.explanation: The distinction spans both mechanism (inheritance vs composition) and scope (one step vs the whole algorithm) — Template Method overrides a piece inside a fixed skeleton, Strategy swaps out the entire behavior. The other options misstate either pattern's actual requirements.

mcqs.question: A requirement states that callers must be able to swap an algorithm's behavior after the object has already been constructed, at runtime. Which pattern fits, and why?
options: Template Method, because subclassing always supports runtime behavior changes
Strategy, because its collaborator is injected and can be swapped on an existing instance, unlike Template Method's compile-time-fixed subclass choice
Either pattern works identically for this requirement
Neither pattern supports changing behavior after construction under any circumstances
mcqs.explanation: Strategy's injected collaborator can be reassigned after construction, satisfying a true runtime-swap requirement; Template Method's variation point is resolved by which subclass was instantiated, which is fixed once the object exists. The two patterns are not interchangeable here, and Strategy specifically does support this case.

mcqs.question: Why is Strategy generally easier to unit test in isolation than Template Method?
options: Because Strategy implementations can be instantiated and tested standalone, and a test double can be injected into the context, without any base-class machinery
Because Template Method classes cannot be compiled without a full application context
Because Strategy interfaces are always simpler than Template Method's abstract classes, regardless of the actual code
Because JUnit does not support testing abstract classes at all
mcqs.explanation: Strategy's variation is a standalone object, easy to construct and inject a test double for; Template Method testing usually goes through a concrete subclass, coupling the test to the inheritance hierarchy. Template Method classes compile and test fine on their own, interface simplicity isn't guaranteed by the pattern itself, and JUnit has no such restriction on abstract classes.

mcqs.question: How does the Hollywood principle ("don't call us, we'll call you") specifically show up in Template Method?
options: The subclass calls the base class's process() method directly whenever it needs new data
Both the base class and subclass must call each other in a synchronized loop
The subclass registers itself as an Observer and waits for the base class to notify it via a callback queue
The base class's fixed method calls into the subclass's overridden step; the subclass never calls back into the base class to ask what to do next
mcqs.explanation: The inversion of control is exactly this: the base class stays in charge and calls into the subclass's override at the point it decides, while the subclass never drives the interaction by calling back into the base class. There's no synchronized loop, no callback queue, and the subclass isn't the one initiating the call.
